title: 2 Samuel 6:12–15
context: 2 Samuel 6:12–15 records the second, successful attempt. Hearing that the LORD has blessed Obed-Edom’s house, David brings the ark to his city with joy. After those carrying it go six paces, he sacrifices an ox and a fattened calf, and he dances before the LORD with all his might wearing a linen ephod, while Israel shouts and sounds the trumpet. The text now speaks of those who "bore" the ark, which suggests it was carried rather than carted, as 1 Chronicles 15 describes. Both traditions see reverent obedience and wholehearted joy belonging together in worship.

verses.text: King David was told, “The LORD has blessed the house of Obed-Edom, and all that belongs to him, because of God’s ark.” So David went and brought up God’s ark from the house of Obed-Edom into David’s city with joy.
verses.arminianNotes: David hears that the LORD has blessed Obed-Edom because of God’s ark, and he brings it to his city with joy. Arminians see David encouraged by the evidence of God’s blessing to try again, this time with renewed care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the parallel account in 1 Chronicles 15 describes the Levites carrying the ark properly. Both traditions see joy returning when worship is offered according to God’s instructions.

verses.text: When those who bore the LORD’s ark had gone six paces, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened calf.
verses.arminianNotes: When those carrying the LORD’s ark have gone six paces, David sacrifices an ox and a fattened calf. Arminians see the sacrifice as a careful act of reverence and thanksgiving, showing that David has learned to approach God’s presence with fear and honor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that "those who bore" the ark suggests it is now carried rather than carted. Both traditions read the sacrifice as marking the procession as worship approached on God’s terms.

verses.text: David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was clothed in a linen ephod.
verses.arminianNotes: David dances before the LORD with all his might, wearing a linen ephod. Arminians see wholehearted, joyful worship, with the king humbling himself to celebrate before God rather than standing on his dignity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. The linen ephod was a simple garment associated with priestly service (compare 1 Samuel 2:18), and interpreters discuss what David’s wearing it meant. Both traditions see the verse as joy and reverence combined, not as worship performed for show.

verses.text: So David and all the house of Israel brought up the LORD’s ark with shouting and with the sound of the trumpet.
verses.arminianNotes: David and all Israel bring up the LORD’s ark with shouting and the sound of the trumpet. Arminians see the whole nation sharing in the celebration, with the joy of the first attempt now joined to obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as the climax of the procession. Both traditions read the scene as the right fulfillment of David’s desire to center Israel’s life on God’s presence, a theme celebrated in psalms such as Psalm 24 and Psalm 132.
